subject: Biology
source: Phase F · FEAT-PF1 — author-original scaffold rows for the highest-volume AQA Y10 biology spec points (8461). Sentence frames, word banks and step ladders are drawn from teaching practice on respiration, photosynthesis, osmosis and the immune system.

sentenceFrames: Water moves from a ______ water concentration to a ______ water concentration.
Because the cell is in a ______ solution, water moves ______ the cell.

wordBank.definition: the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, from a region of high water concentration to a region of low water concentration
a membrane that lets some particles through but not others
the difference in concentration between two regions
swollen and firm because the cell has gained water
limp because the cell has lost water

stepLadder: Identify the water concentration inside and outside the cell.
Decide which way water will move (high to low water concentration).
Use the term 'partially permeable membrane' in your answer.
Describe what happens to the cell (gain or lose water; turgid or flaccid).
Use 'osmosis' as the named process.
commonPitfalls: Saying 'water moves to the higher concentration' — this confuses solute and water concentration.
Calling it diffusion instead of osmosis.
rows.visualAidHint: An arrow diagram with a partially permeable membrane down the middle, water arrows on both sides, makes direction explicit.

sentenceFrames: As temperature increases, the rate of reaction ______.
This is because enzyme and substrate molecules ______.
Above the optimum temperature, the active site ______.
The substrate no longer fits the active site, so the reaction ______.

wordBank.definition: a biological catalyst that speeds up a reaction
the molecule that an enzyme acts on
the part of the enzyme where the substrate binds
the active site has changed shape so the substrate no longer fits
the temperature or pH at which the enzyme works fastest

stepLadder: Describe what happens to rate as temperature rises towards the optimum.
Explain why (kinetic energy / collisions).
Describe what happens at the optimum (rate is fastest).
Describe what happens above the optimum (rate falls).
Explain why using the lock-and-key model (active site changes shape, substrate no longer fits).
commonPitfalls: Saying enzymes are 'killed' at high temperature — they are denatured, not killed.
Forgetting to mention the active site changing shape.
Describing only the increase, not the fall above the optimum.
rows.visualAidHint: A rate-vs-temperature graph with the optimum labelled lets pupils anchor their description to the curve.

sentenceFrames: The vaccine contains a ______ form of the pathogen.
The white blood cells produce ______ in response.
When the person meets the real pathogen, the antibodies are produced ______ and in ______ amounts.

wordBank.definition: a dead or weakened form of a pathogen used to trigger an immune response
a protein produced by white blood cells that locks onto a specific antigen
a molecule on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response
a long-lived white blood cell that remembers how to make a specific antibody
an organism that causes disease

stepLadder: State what the vaccine contains.
Describe what the white blood cells do in response.
Explain that memory cells are formed.
Describe what happens on second exposure to the real pathogen.
Conclude that the person does not become ill.
commonPitfalls: Saying the vaccine 'kills' the disease — vaccines prevent illness, they don't kill anything.
Forgetting memory cells, which are why vaccines give long-term protection.

sentenceFrames: Aerobic respiration uses ______ to break down ______.
It produces ______ and ______, plus a lot of energy.
Anaerobic respiration in muscle cells produces ______, with much less energy.
Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast produces ______ and ______.

wordBank.definition: respiration with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide and water
respiration without oxygen, producing lactic acid (in muscle) or ethanol + CO₂ (in plants and yeast)
the sugar broken down during respiration
the product of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells
anaerobic respiration in yeast, used in brewing and bread-making

stepLadder: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscle cells.
Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast/plants.
Compare the products of each.
Compare the relative amount of energy released.
commonPitfalls: Confusing the products of muscle anaerobic respiration with those of yeast.
Saying anaerobic respiration produces 'no energy' — it produces less, not none.
Forgetting the word 'aerobic' in the question equation.
rows.visualAidHint: A two-column comparison table (aerobic vs anaerobic) with rows for reactants, products and energy yield helps structure the answer.
